question.value: Identify and characterize 183 GHz H2O megamaser emission from AGN already known to host 22 GHz megamaser systems, and compare their spectral and spatial properties to 22 GHz masers.

evidence.quote: We present the results of an ALMA survey to identify 183 GHz H$_2$O maser emission from AGN already known to host 22 GHz megamaser systems.
In this section, we describe the properties of each detection, and we compare the 183 GHz maser line characteristics to those of the 22 GHz masers in the same system.
The data presented in this paper were taken as part of ALMA projects 2017.1.00909.S and 2018.1.00321.S.
The data presented in this paper were taken as part of ALMA projects 2017.1.00909.S and 2018.1.00321.S.
We used ALMA’s Band 5 to observe 20 AGN known to host 22 GHz water megamaser systems and spanning a range of redshifts out to $z \approx 0.05$; the targets are listed in [1](#tab:Observations).

frequencies_and_spectral_setup.value: 4 SPWs: 3 with 122 kHz (~0.2 km s^-1) spanning +/- ~1200 km s^-1; 1 with 2 GHz width and 15.625 MHz (~25 km s^-1) channels. Dual linear polarization (XX, YY).

evidence.quote: Three of the spectral windows were configured to have fine frequency resolution (122 kHz, corresponding to $\sim$0.2 km s$^{-1}$) and to span a total of $\pm$ $\sim$1200 km s$^{-1}$ around the expected locations of the maser lines

The fourth spectral window was wider (2 GHz, corresponding to $\sim$3200 km s$^{-1}$) with coarser channels (15.625 MHz, corresponding to $\sim$25 km s$^{-1}$), and was offset toward lower frequency to capture continuum emission.
All observations recorded only dual linear polarization correlation products (XX, YY), and cross-hand data are not available.

Our survey targets the $3_{1,3}$-$2_{2,0}$ rotational transition in the ground vibrational state of the para-H$_2$O molecule (where the nuclear spins of the two hydrogen atoms are anti-parallel), which has a rest-frame emission frequency of 183.310087 GHz[^3] (cite: Pickett_1998).

There is one additional spectral line detected towards Circinus, which we associate with the HNC ($\text{v}=0$, $\text{J}=2\text{ - }1$) transition with a rest-frame frequency of 181.324758 GHz (cite: Muller_2005).

The other line is weaker and has a more ambiguous identification, but we associate it with the HC$_3$N ($\text{v}=0$, $\text{J}=20\text{ - }19$) transition with a rest-frame frequency of 181.944923 GHz (cite: Muller_2005); the distribution of the HC$_3$N emission is shown in [8](#fig:NGC1068H3CN).

continuum_bandwidth.value: 2 GHz (dedicated continuum SPW for most targets)

evidence.quote: The fourth spectral window was wider (2 GHz, corresponding to $\sim$3200 km s$^{-1}$) with coarser channels (15.625 MHz, corresponding to $\sim$25 km s$^{-1}$), and was offset toward lower frequency to capture continuum emission.

Although ALMA was in a relatively compact (C-4) configuration for the 2018 December observations of Circinus (with a corresponding resolution of $\sim$0.6 arcseconds at 183 GHz), the high signal-to-noise ratio provided by the bright maser lines enables coarse mapping of the 183 GHz system.

angular_resolution.value: ~0.6 arcseconds at 183 GHz (for Circinus); arcsecond-scale nominal beam

evidence.quote: Although ALMA was in a relatively compact (C-4) configuration for the 2018 December observations of Circinus (with a corresponding resolution of $\sim$0.6 arcseconds at 183 GHz), the high signal-to-noise ratio provided by the bright maser lines enables coarse mapping of the 183 GHz system.

Even though the nominal beam size of these ALMA observations is arcsecond-scale, the high signal-to-noise ratios achieved by the strong lines in the Circinus spectrum enable us to carry out coarse mapping of the mas-scale system.

findings_qualitative.value: 183 GHz maser emission is detected in 13 out of 20 targeted AGN known to host 22 GHz megamasers, increasing the number of AGN known to host (sub)millimeter megamasers by a factor of 5.

findings_qualitative.value: 183 GHz emission is systematically fainter in flux density than 22 GHz emission from the same targets (roughly an order of magnitude lower), but isotropic luminosities at 183 GHz and 22 GHz are comparable.

evidence.quote: We find that the 183 GHz emission is systematically fainter than the 22 GHz emission from the same targets, with typical flux densities being roughly an order of magnitude lower at 183 GHz than at 22 GHz.
However, the isotropic luminosities of the detected 183 GHz sources are comparable to their 22 GHz values.

findings_qualitative.value: In 9 of the 13 detections, only a single line complex near the systemic velocity is detected; NGC 1194 and CGCG 074-064 show one additional high-velocity feature, while ESO 269-G012 and Circinus show rich multi-component spectra.

evidence.quote: For the majority (9 out of 13) of our 183 GHz maser detections, the spectrum exhibits only a single, largely featureless line complex located near the systemic velocity of the galaxy.

Of the remaining 4 sources, two (NGC 1194 and CGCG 074-064) have a single additional spectral feature detected at velocities that are offset by several hundred km s$^{-1}$ from the systemic velocity of the galaxy, while the other two (Circinus and ESO 269-G012) exhibit considerably more complex spectral structure.

findings_qualitative.value: In Circinus, visibility modeling spatially resolves the 183 GHz maser distribution (~90 mas x 50 mas), showing the same northeast-blueshifted to southwest-redshifted orientation as the 22 GHz VLBI map and consistent with tracing the disk at larger orbital radii.

evidence.quote: Our map shows that the 183 GHz maser system in Circinus is spatially resolved by these ALMA observations, covering a region that appears to be well-matched in size and shape to the ${\sim}90\text{\,mas} \times 50$ mas distribution of 22 GHz masers.
The 183 GHz masers are consistent with being located in the disk identified at 22 GHz, but at larger orbital radii than are occupied by the 22 GHz disk masers.

claims.hypothesis: AGN known to host 22 GHz H2O megamaser systems also commonly host 183 GHz H2O megamaser emission associated with their circumnuclear accretion disks.
claims.experiment: Conducted an ALMA Band 5 survey of 20 AGN known to host 22 GHz water megamaser systems, imaging spectral cubes around the 183.310087 GHz para-H2O transition.
claims.result: Detected significant (>= 5 sigma across multiple channels) 183 GHz maser emission in 13 of the 20 targets, spatially coincident with the continuum peak where continuum is detected, including a classic triple-peaked disk spectrum in ESO 269-G012.
claims.finding: A substantial population of 183 GHz AGN megamasers exists and is associated with the same edge-on accretion disk material as the 22 GHz population, increasing the number of known (sub)millimeter AGN megamasers by a factor of 5.

evidence.quote: Out of 20 sources observed, we detect significant 183 GHz maser emission from 13; this survey thus increases the number of AGN known to host (sub)millimeter megamasers by a factor of 5.

The survey presented in this paper demonstrates the existence of a population of 183 GHz AGN megamasers that shows every indication of being associated with the same edge-on accretion disk material as the known 22 GHz population.

claims.hypothesis: The radiative output of 183 GHz megamasers in AGN accretion disks is comparable to that of 22 GHz megamasers despite differences in flux density.
claims.experiment: Measured peak flux densities and velocity-integrated fluxes at 183 GHz for all 13 detections, computed isotropic luminosities L_iso, and compared them to published 22 GHz values.
claims.result: 183 GHz flux densities are systematically fainter than 22 GHz flux densities by roughly an order of magnitude, but because the frequency is ~8.2x higher, the isotropic luminosities L_iso are typically within a factor of ~2 of the 22 GHz values.
claims.finding: Assuming similar maser beaming angles, the energy emitted in the 183 GHz transition is comparable to that from the 22 GHz transition.

evidence.quote: Across all targets, we find that the 183 GHz maser emission is systematically fainter than the corresponding 22 GHz emission from the same system (typically by nearly an order of magnitude in flux density).

However, because the emission frequency of the 183 GHz transition is also approximately an order of magnitude higher than that of the 22 GHz transition, the isotropic luminosities at 183 GHz and 22 GHz are comparable (typically within a factor of $\sim$2 of one another).

claims.hypothesis: The strong 183 GHz masers in the Circinus galaxy trace the circumnuclear accretion disk at larger orbital radii than the 22 GHz masers.
claims.experiment: Self-calibrated the Circinus visibilities on the brightest 183 GHz channel (~5 Jy at 561.6 km s^-1) and used dynesty nested sampling to fit point-source positions in each spectral channel, comparing the resulting map to the 22 GHz VLBI map.
claims.result: The 183 GHz masers span a ~90 mas x 50 mas region with blueshifted emission to the northeast and redshifted to the southwest, matching the 22 GHz orientation, with a ~40 mas central gap placing them outside the 22 GHz disk region.
claims.finding: The 183 GHz masers in Circinus are consistent with residing in the accretion disk at larger orbital radii than the 22 GHz disk masers, although positional uncertainties prevent unambiguously ruling out an outflow origin.

evidence.quote: Proceeding with this assumption, we find that the 183 GHz masers live primarily outside of the disk region, with a $\sim$40 mas gap separating the blueshifted and redshifted complexes.
The 183 GHz masers are consistent with being located in the disk identified at 22 GHz, but at larger orbital radii than are occupied by the 22 GHz disk masers.

However, the current large uncertainties in our maser position measurements (relative to the size of the system) ultimately make it difficult to unambiguously distinguish between a disk and outflow origin for the 183 GHz masers in Circinus.

why_this_data.value: Selected 20 AGN already known to host 22 GHz disk megamasers (from Pesce et al. 2015) or strong AGN-associated 22 GHz megamasers to test for 183 GHz maser emission using ALMA Band 5.

evidence.quote: We used ALMA’s Band 5 to observe 20 AGN known to host 22 GHz water megamaser systems and spanning a range of redshifts out to $z \approx 0.05$; the targets are listed in [1](#tab:Observations).

Each of the targeted galaxies was selected either because it was identified as a disk maser by (cite: Pesce_2015), and/or – as in the case of NGC 1068, NGC 1386, Circinus, and NGC 5643 – because it is a strong 22 GHz megamaser source associated with an AGN.

why_this_method.value: Manual calibration was performed on all datasets to include observations that did not pass QA2 and to apply self-calibration uniformly; natural weighting was chosen to maximize point source sensitivity; direct visibility fitting was used for Circinus to achieve super-resolution astrometry via high SNR.

evidence.quote: To maintain uniformity, we thus carry out our own data reduction on all datasets.
We use the default “standard” $(u,v)$-gridding setting in `tclean`, and we specify natural visibility weighting to maximize the point source sensitivity of our images.

With a $\sim$0.6 arcsecond beam and signal-to-noise ratios exceeding 200 for some lines, we expect to achieve relative positional uncertainties of several mas for a number of the maser features in the 183 GHz spectrum.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Using standard ALMA QA2 pipeline products directly (rejected to include non-QA2 datasets and perform self-calibration uniformly)

evidence.quote: Though most of the observations taken as part of these ALMA projects have corresponding quality assurance 2 (QA2) data processing, we also include a handful of observations that did not achieve sufficient sensitivity to pass the QA2 level.
To maintain uniformity, we thus carry out our own data reduction on all datasets.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Line-by-line comparison between 183 GHz and 22 GHz spectra (rejected in favor of qualitative comparison of gross structures due to intrinsic maser variability on ~week timescales and large temporal separation between epochs)

evidence.quote: We note that because these megamaser sources are known to be intrinsically variable on timescales of $\sim$weeks at 22 GHz (cite: Lo_2005), the typically large temporal separation between the observations of the 183 GHz masers presented in this paper and their 22 GHz counterparts from the literature renders a line-by-line comparison of the two spectra potentially fraught.
Instead, we opt here for a somewhat more qualitative comparison, aiming to determine whether the two sets of spectra exhibit comparable gross structures.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Using Hubble law distances for nearby galaxies NGC 5643 and Circinus (rejected in favor of SN Ia and Tully-Fisher distances because Hubble law distances are very uncertain at low redshift)

evidence.quote: Because NGC 5643 is nearby enough that the Hubble law distance is expected to be very uncertain, we instead adopt a Type Ia Supernova distance of $12.4 \pm 0.5$ Mpc to this system from (cite: Burns_2020).

Because Circinus is nearby enough that the Hubble law distance is very uncertain, we instead adopt the Tully-Fisher distance measurement of $4.2 \pm 0.8$ Mpc to this system from (cite: Karachentsev_2013).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Using the targeted flux calibrator J1550+0527 for NGC 5765b (rejected because it was < 0.5 Jy; used gain calibrator J1504+1029 instead)

evidence.quote: The targeted flux density calibrator for NGC 5765b, J1550+0527, was quite weak (flux density less than $\sim$0.5 Jy) at the time of the observation. We thus use the gain calibrator, J1504+1029, to also calibrate bandpass and flux density for NGC 5765b.

limitations_admitted.value: Atmospheric 183 GHz water absorption creates a steep transmission gradient across the spectral windows for low-redshift targets (e.g., Circinus, NGC 1386), which is not compensated when computing the average RMS noise level.

evidence.quote: We note that for our lowest-redshift targets (e.g., Circinus, NGC 1386), the steep transmission gradient caused by the atmospheric 183 GHz line causes the the RMS noise level to change substantially across the spectral windows. We do not attempt to compensate for this effect when computing the RMS, so our estimate is an average value across the entire spectral range.

limitations_admitted.value: Lack of absolute astrometric referencing between the 183 GHz ALMA map and the 22 GHz VLBI map of Circinus requires assuming that the brightest 183 GHz spot (561.6 km s^-1) and 22 GHz spot (566.3 km s^-1) coincide spatially.

evidence.quote: It is plausible that both of these lines originate from the same parcel of masing gas (with the $\sim$5 km s$^{-1}$ difference in velocity then attributable to dynamical evolution during the $\sim$20 years separating the two observations), but the lack of absolute astrometric referencing between the two observations means that we cannot be sure; the relative locations of the 183 GHz maser system and the overplotted 22 GHz disk midline in [3](#fig:Circinus) should thus be understood to be an assumption.

limitations_admitted.value: Large positional uncertainties in the C-4 configuration ALMA observations of Circinus prevent unambiguously distinguishing between a disk and outflow origin for the 183 GHz masers.

evidence.quote: However, the current large uncertainties in our maser position measurements (relative to the size of the system) ultimately make it difficult to unambiguously distinguish between a disk and outflow origin for the 183 GHz masers in Circinus.

limitations_admitted.value: Non-simultaneity between the 183 GHz ALMA observations and literature 22 GHz spectra, combined with maser time variability, prevents strict line-by-line comparisons.

evidence.quote: We note that because these megamaser sources are known to be intrinsically variable on timescales of $\sim$weeks at 22 GHz (cite: Lo_2005), the typically large temporal separation between the observations of the 183 GHz masers presented in this paper and their 22 GHz counterparts from the literature renders a line-by-line comparison of the two spectra potentially fraught.
